Anthropic seems hellbent on making itself one of the most hated companies among white collar workers.

As crucial elections loom in the United States, AI chatbots are dumping political misinformation onto the populace with astonishing confidence.

There’s evidence that the problem is widespread. According to recent reporting by the Washington Post , top AI chatbots are giving horribly flawed information to users asking for voting guides on the midterms. For example, when WaPo tasked ChatGPT with creating a voter guide for all the races and candidates relevant to a resident of Missouri, the chatbot added a Senate seat that isn’t even up for re-election. A similar test for a resident in Wyoming claimed that local politicians running in municipal elections were running for federal seats.

In all, WaPo took a look at 3,000 AI-generated voting guides, which frequently shared false voting information that usually traced back to other AI-generated websites . In other words, the AI chatbots are eating their own slop and passing it off as authoritative election information.

Overall, the paper found chatbots failed to find which congressional district an exact address was located in a whopping 48 percent of the time, while those that did got it wrong 22 percent of the time.

Luckily, the share of users actually querying the chatbots seems to be relatively low. According to a late-October survey by the Pew Research Center, just eight percent of US voters say they’ve used an AI chatbot like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini to look up information relevant to the ballot-box.

While the ideal number would be zero voters in any nation receiving AI-generated election misinformation, it seems in 2026, we’ll have to take what we can get.

Posters take existing paparazzi photos of celebrity men and alter them so that the men are shirtless and, most often, extremely jacked. Lipa, for her part, is seen completely clothed in pants and long jackets — while Turner is unnecessarily strolling about shirtless for no clear reason. Original paparazzi shots show that Turner was clothed in real life.

The deepfakes can be hard to spot because most of the images are in large part real. But if you find yourself wondering why Dua Lipa is dressed in an ankle-sweeping coat while her husband is out sans shirt, the answer is likely because you’re looking at a reality skewed by AI.

Celebrities are shilling AI companies. Lionel Messi, probably among the top five most famous people on Earth right now, just did a World Cup ad campaign for OpenAI. Some genuinely seem to be hooked on the beguiling guidance of the tech. Others just seem to be chasing another big payday. But why does it keep happening, even in the face of massive public backlash?

There are fewer better places to start than with Charles Porch, a man who was recently profiled in New York Magazine , which christened him “OpenAI’s Hollywood Whisperer.”

Porch worked at Instagram for 15 years, where his job was basically convincing cool famous people to use the platform, turning it into the cultural powerhouse that it is today. In 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman hired Porch to do the same thing for ChatGPT. Among his list of A-list stars he’s brought into the AI fold is actress Gwyneth Paltrow, whom he arranged a dinner with Altman in September (after a public freakout about rumors of the dinner caused it to be postponed).

A self-styled “tech optimist,” Porch described himself as “not a business-development guy or the brand guy,” but the “relationships person that’s bringing everyone along on new tech” — with that “everyone” all being in a certain tax bracket and with a certain number of Instagram followers.

So one side of the reason why celebrities are falling for AI? Because there’s a very concerted, moneyed, effort to do that by AI companies. Famous people are often targeted this way. It’s why so many of them end up hiring quack doctors, fall into bizarre cultish beliefs if not join actual cults, or throw away their credibility by siding with a person or brand that is decidedly, overwhelmingly, uncool, or goes against everything they appeared to stand for. (A prime example in Hollywood recently: Martin Scorsese’s endorsement of an AI-storyboarding startup .)

But there’s a darker side to this that an anonymously quoted media executive shines a light on. And that’s the fact that celebrities — actors, especially — are more broke and desperate than ever.

“Right now in Hollywood, only the top people are working,” the executive told NYMag . “It’s why Robert Pattinson is in every project or why Nicole Kidman is literally in everything you watch on TV. The next tier down is not getting jobs.”

You can’t overlook the reason why. The tech industry has helped debilitate the movie industry, in a not dissimilar manner to how platforms like Spotify are a parasite sucking money away from artists. Now AI, another tech industry innovation, is coming along and threatening to be the final nail in the coffin by automating tons of creative work. AI can’t replace human creativity, but it can provide a serviceable substitute. Meanwhile, the very uncertainty that AI casts over the industry is enough to spook the bosses running it and cause them to start pinching pennies. Ergo, less work for all.

Then AI, with its immense wealth and unchecked spending, comes marching into the ruins of what it helped destroyed. An obscene amount of capital is being poured into it, and its shining opulence is enough to blind almost anyone.

Woe is Google. After it starved out publishers with its AI features, it’s now getting a taste of its own medicine.

Shares of its parent company Alphabet took an over 11 percent nosedive on Wednesday, after it disclosed that its AI search features are raking in less money than its traditional search ad model. The steep correction wiped out more than $500 billion in market value .

In its Q3 report, Google reported a quarterly revenue of $127.6 billion, a 25 percent year over year increase. But it’s also spending more, with capital expenditures more than doubling from last year to $51.4 billion, largely thanks to its massive AI investments.

Meanwhile, the growth of its revenue from search seems to be tapering off. It reported a 12 percent year-over-year increase to $63.3 billion, which is less than the 14.5 percent growth it reported in the same period last year.

That’s despite Google Search fielding more queries than ever. Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler admitted in an earnings call, per Search Engine Land , that this was because of “lower monetization we’re seeing in AI Mode,” its AI-powered search experience that works more like a chatbot instead of showing the traditional ten blue links.

It’s an ironic, but perhaps not unforeseen, downturn for Google. When ChatGPT became global phenomenon in late 2022, questions were soon asked regarding if a shift to using chatbots to obtain information over a traditional search engine would topple Google’s ludicrous advertising empire, which earns the company hundreds of billions of dollars each year .

Google responded by developing its own AI features, including its notoriously unreliable AI Overviews , and prominently integrating them into its search engine. This came at the expense of the websites and publishers that its AI models were pilfering from: users were happy to read error-plagued summaries instead of visiting the websites that contained the original information, depriving these sites of clicks and ad revenues. Despite Google’s repeated claims to the contrary, multiple studies have demonstrated that AI Overviews have destroyed click-through rates .

This has had a disastrous effect on the media landscape, with data compiled by Axios showing that the number of visits to top news sites plummeted from over 70 million visitors a month in July of 2024 — the year that Google launched AI Overviews — to just over 47 million in July of 2026. Media leaders who responded to a Reuters Institute survey are grim about the future , predicting traffic to their websites to fall by nearly half over the next three years amidst this AI-dominated paradigm.

Now, Google is getting a taste of this too, earning less advertising dollars from its AI Mode than from the traditional search that it is so eager to abandon. It seemingly hasn’t considered what comes next after the websites it earns money off of all go out of business.

Chief business officer Schindler, though, was adamant that Google will soon start squeeze more money out of AI Mode.

“On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent,” he argued. “In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time.”

Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces.

The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.”

Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.”

In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear.

The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language.

The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments.

Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.”

In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all.

Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?”

To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool.

The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others.

It’s become increasingly clear that AI companies are losing the public in their efforts to build enormous and polluting data centers. The topic has turned into a divisive, bipartisan issue looming over the heads of politicians, who’ve largely sided with the corporate interests of Big Tech during this week’s midterm elections in the United States.

The AI industry’s desperate need for a rebrand is more palpable than ever as protests grow and elected officials face the ire of fed up residents at packed community meetings . As such, AI leaders have been pondering how to win over the public, with Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian warning that “we gotta figure out a new narrative on this data center thing” in a tweet earlier this year.

As Axios reports , they’re now reaching for desperate — and borderline comical — measures to recapture the narrative. According to the publication, OpenAI is gearing up to “unleash a policy and PR blitz” as soon as the midterm elections conclude by rebranding data centers with a ludicrously euphemistic moniker: “AI compute campuses.”

“You can try to chase the moment, or seek to inform the moment via the power of ideas,” OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios .

Needless to say, it’s probably as much of a nonstarter as president Donald Trump’s bizarre efforts to rename AI to “super intelligence,” or SI, in a thinly-veiled attempt to test the loyalty of AI leaders .

OpenAI is looking to pave over its fundamentally fractured relationship with the public by arguing that data centers can “transform host communities” and bring “thousands of jobs,” per Axios , in widely disputed claims that conveniently gloss over the fact that those benefits rarely stick around once construction is complete.

The downsides of the AI industry’s gargantuan push to build data centers are near impossible to ignore. Many operators are taking advantage of regulatory loopholes — and an amenable political environment — to rely on diesel generators, sending emissions skyrocketing . They require major swathes of land to be cleared of vegetation , push local residents out , and consume copious amounts of water , much of which can’t be reclaimed. Many also emit a deafening screeching noise that make living near them a living hell.

The upside, especially for rural Americans, are thin. In short, especially with a potential political sea change on the horizon, OpenAI is trying to figure out a way to meet the moment, as Lehane told Axios .

“AI is going to be the issue in 2028,” he added, referring to this week’s midterm elections as a “bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.”

However, trying to rename data centers to “AI compute campuses,” a term we’re willing to bet will be ignored outright and forgotten almost immediately, isn’t going to change anybody’s mind.

What’s next? Will OpenAI try to rebrand “climate change” as well?

Michigan is set to deploy a major new AI system to prisons across the state, meant to classify incarcerated people based on “how dangerous they are.”

That’s according to Detroit channel Fox2 , which reports that the Michigan Department of Corrections is plowing ahead with an inmate categorization algorithm that will sort people into various housing levels.

In Michigan, incarcerated people are separated into five housing levels according to their security classification. In the past, screenings were performed by a committee of staff appointed by the Warden at each facility. Now, it seems the state wants to outsource that decision — or at least have it be heavily informed by — a non-profit tech company called Recidiviz.

Recidiviz began as a data organization project at Google, meant to “uncover how technology could standardize criminal justice data and improve the system nationwide.” Its AI-integrated software platform is said to perform features like identifying individuals eligible for state-offered programs, reclassification, or release, and coordinate access to resources like transitional housing and employment.

In a press release , MDOC said the Recidiviz software will be used to “optimize placement of incarcerated individuals” starting with a pilot program in a number of men’s facilities beginning in December. The state agency notes that the AI tool is expected to “improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30 percent,” though how the state arrived at that vague figure is unclear.

For incarcerated people, housing designations are extremely consequential, determining which programming and resources an incarcerated person is eligible for, and what kind of population they’ll be housed with for the duration of their sentence.

Setting the state’s rationale aside, the MDOC-Recividiz partnership leaves some major questions unanswered.

What kind of data will be collected, for example, will matter a great deal with regard to the AI system’s accuracy. As a ProPublica investigation into a similar risk-analysis program in Louisiana found, the kind of data being used to classify incarcerated people contained inherent racial and socioeconomic bias.

As a result, Louisiana’s carceral system has become even more cruel and harmful to those earnestly working toward rehabilitation. In one case reported by ProPublica , a blind and wheelchair bound 70-year-old was determined to be a “moderate risk” of reoffending despite having a clean disciplinary record — a classification which results in an automatic loss of eligibility for parole.

While Michigan’s system is geared toward housing assignments rather than parole decisions, it seems highly unlikely that software alone will solve the state’s ongoing corrections crisis — and if Louisiana’s embrace of AI is any example, it could very well make matters far, far worse.

Michigan Department of Corrections was contacted for comment.

AI companies sure have a funny marketing strategy.

When they’re not too busy predicting how their own tech will destroy the world , they like to insist that AI is well on its way to — or already has — surpassed the cognitive ability of humans. They’re grabbing customers by the shoulders, looking them dead in the eye, and telling them that they’ve now been rendered inferior beings. They’ll be honored, they seem to believe, to be a stepping stone towards progress (or tortured for eternity by a vindictive superintelligence for trying to stop AI from being brought about, according to certain utterly delusional corners of Silicon Valley.)

And that brings us to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Speaking at a conference in Abu Dhabi this week, Altman, whose company is under fire right now for allegedly disrespecting the entire field of mathematics , stressed that people should remain in control of the future, not AI. That’s when he snuck in a little side claim: that AI has now eclipsed even the brightest scientists — hence why it’s more urgent than ever that we keep a handle on our own destiny.

At the start of this year, “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists. And now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Altman said at the conference, in conversation with the editor-in-chief of the UAE state-owned paper The National .

Altman and OpenAI have long banged on about the intelligence of its models with respect to human scholars. When it released GPT-5 last year, it touted it as having “PhD-levels” of intelligence, and was routinely mocked for that obviously not being the case. Altman has also frequently predicted that AI will surpass human intelligence by the end of the decade.

This year, the “PhD-level” claim actually appeared to come true, sort of. OpenAI announced that it found a solution to the Navier-Stokes equations as laid out in the famous Millennium Prize Problems, something no human mathematician had ever solved. That caused a blowup ( get it? ) because a mathematician accused OpenAI of unfairly using his research, fueling discussions about how OpenAI was treating the math community.

OpenAI then poured fuel on the tire — or should we say, threw tons of paper on it — by simultaneously releasing hundreds of studies documenting purported solutions to even more math problems. Prominent mathematicians were incensed at how the community was being treated as unpaid proofreaders for OpenAI’s mountain of output, while OpenAI got to glorify their model as already matching their human intellect.

For Altman to come out and say that AI is now smarter than scientists when he has a significant chunk of the scientific community gunning for him is, shall we say, a choice. It’s also a claim that needs proof. The math fiasco is a good example of why it remains dubious. While the solutions appear technically correct, the actual natural language of the AI proofs are borderline incomprehensible , and it will probably take researchers years to unpack them all. As such, their actual utility to the field remains questionable.

From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear.

In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated.

As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation.

“I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar .

Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months.

In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name.

In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies.

As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.”

Despite a visibly degrading job market and widespread anxiety around AI automation, empirical evidence definitively linking the two phenomena has been hard to come by. Until now, at least.

New reporting by the Financial Times details two new sources of data pointing to AI’s impact on the labor market.

First, there was a new analysis by US-based financial researcher Eric Basmajian, who recently wrote in a post on social media that “AI productivity gains are showing up” in jobs data — with the caveat that only about 15 percent of jobs seem to be impacted so far.

“The three heaviest AI adopters (information, professional services, finance) went from a 2.2 percent productivity trend to 5.0 percent since 2022,” Basmajian explained, pointing to incremental gains in workplace productivity coinciding with a high AI adoption rate.

The very next day after Basmajian’s post, what appears to be an internal Goldman Sachs report began circulating on social media. It warned that the “AI labor market impact” has been spreading beyond tech work — a field that has already been hit hard as generative AI becomes a common tool for writing software code.

The report shows a rising trend between an industry’s AI exposure and unemployment around non-tech professional sectors like finance, telecomms, technical services, and administration, seemingly reinforcing Basmajian’s assertion.

But while there does seem to be a positive trendline in at least some areas of the job market, the FT tacks on a veritable laundry list of disclaimers.

Perhaps most importantly, the metrics looking at “productivity” in these cases aren’t necessarily reflective of quality — meaning we’re not necessarily talking about skyrocketing productive output and revenue as a result of AI, but of lower headcount, which is a big difference.

The data is also specifically about the US, pointing to broader post-Pandemic economic woes rather than a global AI jobpocalypse. As the FT explains, the “link that was visible in the US between AI usage on the one hand, and productivity growth and falling employment on the other, is conspicuously absent elsewhere.”

Either way, it seems the AI doomers finally have something to write home about as far as the labor market is concerned — though anyone preparing their bunker for a hypothetical AI labor revolution is going to have to keep on waiting.

Schools across the country have long grown dependent on Google, from its eponymous search engine to services like Gmail and Chromebooks, the company’s cheap laptops that have become commonplace in classrooms.

But it’s a fraught relationship that’s now seriously being tested as teachers start to suspect that the AI use is wreaking havoc on the impressionable minds of their students. The tech has been shown to erode young people’s critical thinking skills , cause their testing skills to plummet , and — at the extreme end — drive them into isolation and AI psychosis .

Google is now putting on brass knuckles to keep its AI in schools, saying that it’ll be unwilling to support schools that move to block AI entirely. As the New York Times reports , the tech giant is revoking access to Google Search, the most important gateway to information on the open web, for any schools looking to restrict AI.

It’s a spiteful move that could greatly deteriorate the company’s already tenuous relationship with educators. Put differently, Google is holding schools hostage by withholding its number one bargaining chip from any institution willing to say no to AI. The decision could force teachers’ and administrators’ hands as they watch AI destroy a generation of students .

Google has plastered “AI Overviews” on top of its search engine, entangling the two products. But the service’s answers are its frequently wrong, turning the very top of company’s index of the internet into a massive minefield of misinformation .

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Google VP of education Chris Phillips told the NYT . If a school bans AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The company has been advertising its Gemini AI chatbot to schools as a way to help teachers and provide personalized tutors to students. It forced the AI features on classrooms earlier this year by making them the default, triggering a major outcry among educators.

The news comes as state regulators continue to ponder how to set rules for the use of AI in public education and by minors as a whole. Several school districts across New York and California have restricted some of these features on school devices, with the hopes of regaining access to traditional search without AI Overviews.

But that option no longer appears to be on the table as Google looks to force AI into classrooms. The company announced this week that schools can either choose to have search with AI Overviews turned on — or a student-oriented version of its Gemini chatbot, called Guided Learning.

Those two options are unlikely to get a glowing reception from frustrated educators looking to protect children from the many harmful effects of AI.

For years now, some of the biggest players in the AI space have been investing in smaller startups — which in turn use the same exact money to purchase services from the same large companies.

Investors have watched this circular financing with quiet but growing trepidation. After all, as the Wall Street Journal points out , if the AI bubble were to pop, the consequences could be dire. Now, with fears over a sudden collapse are as palpable as ever, such a “tangled web of AI bets,” as the newspaper puts it, could spell disaster.

The signs aren’t exactly hard to identify. Just last week, Google’s parent company Alphabet experienced the biggest drop in its market value in its history, wiping out well over half a trillion dollars in value .

The accompanying crash likely didn’t just send jitters across tech markets. Since the AI industry is effectively propping up the entire US economy, its failure could have far-reaching consequences to a public that’s increasingly skeptical of its offerings .

Since most of these companies’ fates are inextricably linked by circular financing, a major economic downturn or weakening demand could have cascading repercussions, especially considering much of the sector’s financing is based on debt.

Beyond the tech industry’s very bad week, data center operators aren’t looking much better. Nvidia customer CoreWave, which analysts have dubbed the “ AI trade’s canary in the coal mine ,” has also seen its shares decline over months, raising plenty of flags .

Despite the widespread unease, enormous data center expansion efforts are in full swing, major bipartisan backlash notwithstanding. It’s an unprecedented all-in that could jeopardize the entire economy if it were to collapse.

Even beyond the US, the circular financing is starting to worry investors sweat in Asia. The Bank of Korea recently warned of a “semiconductor version of Dutch disease,” an economic concept describing a booming sector that overtakes all other tradable market segments.

Yet the country is doubling down, with president Lee Jae Myung pledging today to “boldly invest in AI and future growth engines,” effectively doubling AI and chip spending for next year.

Only time will tell whether that’ll be the right move as more and more investors get cold feet.

AI robots couldn’t let us keep our vanity to ourselves. They’re now hitting the gym, too — but the reps they’re getting in aren’t of the weightlifting kind.

Enter Neura, a buzzy robotics startup in Metzingen, Germany, that is positioning itself at the forefront of embodied AI by training these advanced systems to inhabit and navigate the real world.

According to a new piece from the New York Times , the heart of its operations is its secretive “robogym” facility in Munich, where up to one hundred humanoids from companies around the world constantly practice and perform tasks — from chores to factory work — so they can get better at them.

The NYT described the scene, in the first time a journalist has been given access to the facility: “The robots picked up car parts and placed them into containers, stacked boxes and carried out other tasks, mimicking the movements of human trainers who guided them remotely. One robot practiced tightening its grip on a glass, learning how to respond when water is added.”

Large language models can draw on existing data, from internet posts to books, to “learn” about the world. But the equivalent corpus of data doesn’t exist for the physical world, so it has to be created and collected .

Neura founder David Reger likened it to learning to swim, telling the NYT that you can’t simply watch videos; you have to get in the water.

Having recently raised up to $1.4 billion from the likes of Nvidia and Amazon in a June funding round, Neura is gunning to become something like the Gold’s Gym of the robo world. By the end of next year, per the NYT , it plans to operate five gyms across the globe. It already has one in Hangzhou, China, one of the country’s major tech hubs.

It’s a leader in the West, but it’s playing catch up with Chinese competitors, who altogether already run more than 90 humanoid data collection centers, according to data from the consulting firm Interact Analysis, while Europe only has ten.

Currently, most robots used in factories are specialized for specific tasks. Humanoid robots aim to be versatile like a real employee, but are harder to pull off. There’s still huge questions over their, but the idea seems to making some headway, with BMW preparing to trial robots from the Swiss company Hexagon Robotics on the factory floor. Japan Airlines is also experimenting with robot baggage handlers at Tokyo’s Haneda airport, who presumably have had plenty of time to hit the gym.
